node.label: Dipesh Chakrabarty
node.date_label: Rethinking Working-Class History 1989 · “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” 1992 · Provincializing Europe 2000 · “The Climate of History” 2009
node.description: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective who argues that 'Europe' remains 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”'. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that 'interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. After 2000, 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Dipesh Chakrabarty (b. 1948); Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” (Representations, 1992); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (Perspectives, 1997); Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000); “Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital” (Public Culture, 2000). After 2000: “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (Critical Inquiry, 2009). Readings: Nair’s review (1990); Dirlik (1994); Chandavarkar (1997); Sarkar (1997); Whose Anthropocene? (2016), with his response.
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1989 preface (pp. xi–xv) and introduction (pp. 3–6) in the publisher preview; 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (Representations 37, 1992, pp. 1–26) in full; the 1997 AHA essay in full (web text, no page numbers); the Provincializing Europe introduction (pp. 3–23, in the publisher’s excerpt); 'Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital' (Public Culture, 2000), which he describes as a slightly different version of the book’s chapter 2; and 'The Climate of History' (2009) in full. The rest of the 1989 and 2000 books is unread, including chapter 2 itself. He is not presented as a founder. He calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group' (1997) and writes that his 'argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (2000, p. 15). The book’s critique of historicism builds on Guha’s rejection of Hobsbawm’s 'prepolitical' and cites Fabian’s 'denial of coevalness' (pp. 8, 11–15). Contested in period: by Sarkar (1997), by Chandavarkar (1997) and, in a critique aimed mainly at Prakash, by Dirlik (1994). The 2009 essay and its reception (2014–16) are after 2000 and support only the separate environment edge, which is marked post_2000; they are not evidence for any claim about his work before 2000.

proposed_edges.relationship: Provincializing Europe: Europe as the silent referent of historical knowledge, the historicism of 'first in Europe, then elsewhere', and European categories held to be both indispensable and inadequate (1992–2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History', Representations 37 (1992), pp. 1–26, read in full (the hosted copy's text layer runs words together; spacing restored in quotations): 'insofar as the academic discourse of history ... is concerned, “Europe” remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan,” and so on'; '“Indian” history itself is in a position of subalternity' (p. 1). 'That Europe works as a silent referent in historical knowledge itself becomes obvious in a highly ordinary way': 'Third-world historians feel a need to refer to works in European history; historians of Europe do not feel any need to reciprocate' (p. 2). The everyday paradox is that 'we find these theories, in spite of their inherent ignorance of “us,” eminently useful in understanding our societies' (p. 3). 'Let us call this the project of provincializing “Europe”' (p. 20); it 'does not call for a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity, liberal values, universals, science, reason, grand narratives, totalizing explanations' (p. 20), and 'must realize within itself its own impossibility' (p. 22). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 3–23 read in the publisher's excerpt: historicism 'made modernity or capitalism look ... as something that became global over time, by originating in one place (Europe) and then spreading outside it. This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); it 'came to non-European peoples in the nineteenth century as somebody's way of saying “not yet” to somebody else', and Mill's argument 'consigned Indians, Africans, and other “rude” nations to an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8). European thought 'is both indispensable and inadequate', and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'provincializing Europe is not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16). The problem of capitalist modernity is 'a problem of translation, as well' as of transition (p. 17). Chapter 1 'reproduces, in an abridged form, a programmatic statement ... that I published in 1992 in the journal Representations' (p. 19). In-period reception and criticism: Arif Dirlik (Critical Inquiry 20, 1994; read) cites the 1992 essay (p. 334, n. 7) for postcolonial criticism's repudiation of the modes-of-production narrative, and objects that 'The denial of capitalism's foundational status also reveals a culturalism in the postcolonialist argument': 'Without capitalism as the foundation for European power and the motive force of its globalization, Eurocentrism would have been just another ethnocentrism' (p. 346). Dirlik's main target is Gyan Prakash; Chakrabarty appears only in his notes (nn. 7, 12). A contribution, not a founding: the book's epigraph takes 'provincialized' from Gadamer (p. 3), and the post entry already maps Said and Spivak; his argument 'follows directly from my involvement' in Subaltern Studies (p. 15). edge_096 (post → modern) and edge_124 (post → global) stay: they record the group's critiques, which already name him.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: provincializing ('Provincializing historical categories'; 'Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model'; works: Provincializing Europe, 2000) holds him alone and matches the checked argument. The strand's works field could add the 1992 Representations essay at release.

proposed_edges.relationship: Subaltern pasts and the limits of the historian's translation: a member's critique of the transition narrative within Subaltern Studies (1992–2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts', Perspectives (AHA), November 1997, read in full (web text, no page numbers; the live page refused automated access, so the July 2024 Internet Archive capture of the same URL was read): 'Let me call these histories subordinated or “subaltern” pasts'; they are 'pasts that resist historicization'; 'what differentiates the Subaltern Studies project from the older tradition of “history from below” is the self-critical awareness of this problem'. Reading Guha's 'Prose of Counter-Insurgency' on the Santal rebellion of 1855, he writes that 'the historian as historian, unlike the Santal, cannot invoke the supernatural in explaining/describing an event'; the Santal statement 'has to be anthropologized ... before it finds a place in the historian's narrative'; 'Begun in an oppositional mode, “minority histories” can end up being additional instances of “good history.”' 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992, read in full) turns the critique on the collective: the transition narrative 'can be located in our own work in the Subaltern Studies project. My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' (p. 4); the project's founding statement shows 'The tendency to read Indian history in terms of a lack, an absence, or an incompleteness' (p. 5). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction (read): Guha's critique of the category 'prepolitical' 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 14), and the book 'elaborates some of the theoretical concerns that have arisen out of my involvement in Subaltern Studies, but it is not an attempt to represent the life practices of the subaltern classes' (p. 20). In-period criticism from inside the collective: Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 84–85, 87 and 97 checked against the page images) quotes Chakrabarty's account of a shift from the attempt 'to write “better” Marxist histories' to the problem of 'universalism/Eurocentrism' and argues 'that the trajectory that has been outlined with considerable precision and frankness by Chakrabarty has been debilitating in both academic and political terms' (pp. 84–85); he asks of Chakrabarty's reading of Bengali domestic ideals, 'Beauty, pleasure, the good life ... for whom, it is surely legitimate to ask' (p. 97). The words Sarkar quotes come from Chakrabarty's 'Marx after Marxism' (1993), which was not read. A contribution, not a founding: in 1997 he calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group'. edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_392 (subaltern → truthdebate) stay; the 1997 essay's engagement with Telling the Truth About History remains on edge_392.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: historical_translation ('Historical translation and its limits'; 'Religious accounts of agency pose a problem for the secular historian’s narration'; work: 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts', 1997) holds him alone and matches the checked 1997 argument and the 2000 framing of transition as translation. subaltern/labor is carried by edge 3; internal_criticism is Sarkar's strand.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bengal jute-mill workers against universal class narratives: culture, hierarchy and the assumption of bourgeois equality in Marx's 'capital' (1989), taken up and contested by labour historians (1990–97)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own statement of the book's aim. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989), preface pp. xi–xv and introduction pp. 3–6, read in the publisher preview (imprint: copyright 1989; first paperback printing 2000; preface dated February 1988): 'In looking at this history in terms of Marx's categories, however, my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; 'there is an assumption regarding “culture” built into Marx's category of “capital,” and much of what I have to say on Indian labor history, and labor history in general, follows from this reading of Marx' (p. xi); 'this book is an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis of culture, the 'common sense' of Marxist labour history in India; 'Culture, one might say, is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii). 'Perhaps we have long overestimated capitalism's need or capacity to homogenize the cultural conditions necessary for its own reproduction' (p. xiii). He keeps a commitment to equality: 'The struggle to be a “citizen” must be part of the struggle to be a “comrade”' (p. xiv). The figure of the worker in Marx 'was that of a person who belonged to a society where the bourgeois notion of equality was ingrained in culture' (p. 3), and 'there is no “working class” or “working-class consciousness” that ... “is either transcendental in relation to the field of events or runs in its empty sameness throughout the course of history”' (p. 6, quoting Foucault). He separates his argument from Thompson's: 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9). In-period reception by labour historians: Janaki Nair's review in International Labor and Working-Class History 37 (1990, pp. 96–99; not re-read here; the graph's verification note records that she recognises the theoretical contribution while questioning cultural determination, the treatment of traditions as survivals and the analysis of gender). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, '“The Making of the Working Class”: E. P. Thompson and Indian History', History Workshop Journal 43 (1997; written for the 1994 History Workshop conference on Thompson; pp. 177–196 read): Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization of a “traditional” Indian, implicitly “Hindu” culture — in Bengal, a predominantly Muslim province' (p. 182); 'Bengali society, indeed Indian society, was now represented as England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); the view 'recently restated by Dipesh Chakrabarty, that rural migrants “imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting”' 'was not the product of an extensive investigation of the nature of labour migration' (pp. 184–185). Sarkar (1997, p. 87, page image checked) calls these 'stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history'. In 1992 he wrote that 'My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4). Context, not a genealogy: Eric Hobsbawm is among those he thanks for reading the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xvii). edge_742 (subaltern → labourhistory) names him and Nair; see the proposed relabel. edge_358 (subaltern → social) stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: colonial_categories ('Colonial labour, culture, caste and criticism'; 'Chakrabarty’s Bengal interpretation receives Nair’s criticism') holds him with Kumar, Nair and Cooper and matches the checked argument and its criticism. A reviewer could add Chandavarkar (1997) to the strand at release; he has no people record yet.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's 'prepolitical' peasant as an instance of the historicism Western Marxism cultivated: the critique Guha began (1983), extended in Provincializing Europe (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own text. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 11–15 read in the publisher's excerpt: 'Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” revealed the limits of how far historicist Marxist thought could go in responding to the challenge posed to European political thought by the entry of the peasant into the modern sphere of politics' (p. 11). Hobsbawm 'readily admitted' the importance of peasants' 'acquisition of political consciousness' but 'missed the implications of this observation for the historicism that already underlay his own analysis'; in 'Hobsbawm's historicist language, the social movements of the peasants of the twentieth century remained “archaic”' (pp. 11–12). 'The analytical impulse of Hobsbawm's study belongs to a variety of historicism that Western Marxism has cultivated since its inception', including the language of 'survivals' and 'remnants' and 'variations on the theme of “uneven development”' (p. 12). The Hobsbawm passages he quotes are referenced in the book's notes 35–36, which are not in the excerpt; which Hobsbawm work they cite was not checked. He credits the critique to Guha: Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”' in English-language Marxist historiography, 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11). He keeps Marx: 'Marx is critical for the enterprise' (p. 18), and in 1992 Marx 'remains ... a relevant and fundamental critic of both capitalism and liberalism' ('Artifice', p. 4). The same argument appears in Public Culture (2000, p. 670): read historically, Marx's 'not yet' 'refers us back to the idea of history as a waiting room ... the period to which the Third World is often consigned'. A counter-critique from a labour historian, in period: Chandavarkar (1997) writes that 'Thompson has been poorly represented by his disciples among the Subaltern historians' (p. 182). No in-period reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The eric_hobsbawm person entry has no strands. The critique concerns his category 'prepolitical', which no entry currently maps (the atlas has Labouring Men, Bandits and the nationalism work); social/bandit_debate is the nearest strand but concerns his bandit model, not the prepolitical category.
proposed_edges.include_note: Targets the person entry because the passage names Hobsbawm. The same pages generalise to 'a variety of historicism that Western Marxism has cultivated'; a reviewer who prefers the group could retarget the edge to marx (Marxist social history), where Hobsbawm and Thompson hold the labour strand.

proposed_edges.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Post-2000 edge (user decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break); no claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) finds it 'more radical than even he intended' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here only through his response; their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No environment strand covers climate change or the Anthropocene; the node's frame (1970s consolidation, coverage through 2000) predates the essay. ecological_exchange (Crosby, Melville) is the strand his essay argues against, not one it belongs to. A reviewer could add a strand at the rebuild (for example, 'Climate, geological agency and the limits of historical understanding').
proposed_edges.include_note: Drafted on the coordinator's instruction of 2026-10-14 (the user ended the 2000 break). The applier's EDGE_KEYS do not copy post_2000 into the packet; the flag lives in this draft until the rebuild sets a convention.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. The 1992 essay names 'development, modernization, capitalism' as themes of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4), and the 2000 introduction criticises 'stagist' theories 'ranging from simple evolutionary schemas to sophisticated understandings of “uneven development”' (p. 9). Neither text engages the modernization theorists on the modern roster (Rostow, Lerner, Parsons and others). edge_096 (post → modern, critique) already names him and rests on the same introduction; it stays.
Folded into edge 4. The checked passage names Hobsbawm and generalises to Western Marxism (2000, p. 12). Edge 4 targets the eric_hobsbawm person entry; retargeting it to marx is the alternative.

He has a social roster row and two social strands, and edge_358 (subaltern → social, critique) names him. The labour edge (edge 3) carries the argument with labour-history reception (Nair in ILWCH, Chandavarkar in History Workshop Journal); a second arrow to social would repeat it. edge_358 stays.
The 1997 essay discusses Telling the Truth About History at length (read). edge_392 (subaltern → truthdebate) already records that engagement and names him; a person edge would duplicate it.

edge_124 (post → global, critique) names him and stays. The 2009 essay argues with Geyer and Bright's 'World History in a Global Age' (pp. 213–214, 221–222), but that is post-2000 and concerns world-historical universals; it could be drafted at the rebuild.

The 2000 introduction calls Fanon's struggle to hold on to the Enlightenment idea of the human 'part of the global heritage of all postcolonial thinkers' (p. 5). edge_088 (anticolonial → post) and edge_147 (fanon → post) already rest on this page; the direction runs from Fanon to postcolonial criticism, not from Chakrabarty outward.

The original brief asked for this pair to be recorded here as deferred to the rebuild. The coordinator's update of 2026-10-14 (the user ended the 2000 break) replaced that instruction: it is drafted as edge 5, marked post_2000.

proposed.relationship: Subaltern Studies accounts of colonial workers' culture and consciousness taken into labour history, and contested there by labour historians (1989–97)
proposed.map_label: Subaltern accounts of workers' culture, contested, 1989–97
proposed.evidence_note: In-period evidence: Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, History Workshop Journal 43 (1997), pp. 177–196, read. 'While, at first, the subaltern historians borrowed liberally from Thompson's ideas, rhetoric and example, they seemed to take little account of wider developments in social history' (p. 182). 'The Subaltern followers of Thompson' espoused the view that rural migrants 'imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting' (p. 184), and 'some Subaltern historians mistook the received wisdom and commonplace of colonial officials for interpretative novelty' (p. 185); his note cites Arnold's 'Industrial Violence' as well as Chakrabarty (n. 32). Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions cultural determination and the treatment of gender (graph verification note; not re-read in 1.132). The arrow records one collective's labour histories and the criticism they drew in labour-history venues; it does not claim that labour history adopted the subaltern approach. Chakrabarty's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.132).

edge_742.alternative: Leave edge_742 unchanged if reviewers read it as the subaltern entry's contribution, with Chakrabarty and Nair as its example.

new_sources.title: Dipesh Chakrabarty, “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?”, Representations 37 (Winter 1992): 1–26.
new_sources.citation: Dipesh Chakrabarty, “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?”, Representations 37, Special Issue: Imperial Fantasies and Postcolonial Histories (Winter 1992): 1–26. doi:10.1525/rep.1992.37.1.99p0090f.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 1–26, text and notes) in a copy of the JSTOR PDF (JSTOR cover sheet: Representations 37, pp. 1–26, stable URL 2928652). The text layer runs words together; quotations restore word spacing and were checked against the page order. OpenAlex W2079601464 and the DOI agree (Representations 37:1, 1992, pp. 1–26). Passages used: 'Europe' as 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories'; 'Indian' history 'in a position of subalternity' (p. 1); 'a silent referent in historical knowledge'; the asymmetry of ignorance (p. 2); theories 'eminently useful' despite their ignorance of 'us' (p. 3); Marx as 'a relevant and fundamental critic of both capitalism and liberalism'; the transition narrative 'in our own work in the Subaltern Studies project. My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' (p. 4); 'a lack, an absence, or an incompleteness' (p. 5); the subject 'spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative' (p. 19); 'the project of provincializing “Europe”', not 'a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity' (p. 20); its 'own impossibility' (p. 22). Note 1 identifies the praise he questions on p. 1 as Ronald Inden's (1986).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period essay: the first statement of the provincializing argument, reprinted in abridged form as chapter 1 of Provincializing Europe (2000).

OpenAlex W2084393312 gives the DOI and HWJ 43:1, pp. 177–196; the download stamp cites academic.oup.com/hwj/article-abstract/43/1/177/835223. Note 1: written for the History Workshop conference 'E. P. Thompson and the Uses of History', London, 8–9 July 1994. Passages used: subaltern historians 'borrowed liberally from Thompson's ideas'; 'Thompson has been poorly represented by his disciples among the Subaltern historians'; Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization' (p. 182; the scan's OCR reads 'Iiindu' for 'Hindu'); 'England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); rural migrants 'imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting', a view 'not the product of an extensive investigation' (pp. 184–185); 'received wisdom and commonplace of colonial officials' (p. 185); the Saidian turn and 'an active presence in the whole process of disciplining' (pp. 190–191). Notes 24–25 and 30–31 cite Rethinking Working-Class History, pp. xii–xiii and other pages.

verification.note: Open PDF (122 pp.) read in part: contents, foreword and introduction (pp. 5–8), LeCain's essay (pp. 15–20) and Chakrabarty's response (pp. 103–108). The foreword dates the workshop to February 2015 at the University of South Carolina, co-sponsored by the Rachel Carson Center. Passages used: the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7); it challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8); LeCain: 'more radical than even he intended' (p. 15), 'it becomes reasonable to ask whether there was ever a divide in the first place' (p. 17); Chakrabarty concedes the separation of biological and geological agency (p. 104) and reports criticism by Malm and Hornborg and by McAfee over 'lifeboats for the rich' (p. 108). The other contributions were not read. Malm and Hornborg, 'The geology of mankind?', Anthropocene Review 1:1 (2014), 62–69, doi:10.1177/2053019613516291, is closed access and unread.

post.note: Whole introduction, 'The Idea of Provincializing Europe', pp. 3–23, re-read for the 1.132 person entry (pagination of the publisher's excerpt; the excerpt has no imprint page). Quoted: Gadamer epigraph on Europe 'provincialized' (p. 3); 'indispensable and inadequate' and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'first in the West, and then elsewhere' (pp. 6–7); 'This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); 'not yet' and 'an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8); Hobsbawm's 'prepolitical' and Guha's criticism of it (pp. 11–14); 'a variety of historicism that Western Marxism has cultivated since its inception' (p. 12); Guha's critique 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power' (p. 14); 'My argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (p. 15); 'not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16); transition as 'a problem of translation, as well' (p. 17); 'Marx is critical for the enterprise' (p. 18); chapter 1 reproduces the 1992 Representations statement (p. 19); 'not an attempt to represent the life practices of the subaltern classes' (p. 20). The notes and the rest of the book are not in the excerpt.

subaltern.note: Read in full for the 1.132 person entry in the Internet Archive capture of 16 July 2024 of the AHA page (byline Dipesh Chakrabarty; Publication Date November 1, 1997; Perspectives Section Viewpoints); the live page returned 403 to automated requests. Web text, no page numbers. Quoted: minority histories becoming 'additional instances of “good history”'; 'Let me call these histories subordinated or “subaltern” pasts'; 'pasts that resist historicization'; Guha as 'the founder of the group'; Subaltern Studies differs from 'history from below' by 'the self-critical awareness of this problem'; the Santal statement 'has to be anthropologized'; 'the historian as historian, unlike the Santal, cannot invoke the supernatural in explaining/describing an event'.

chakrabarty_labour.note: Publisher preview re-read for the 1.132 person entry, adding the introduction pp. 3–6 and acknowledgments pp. xvii–xviii to the preface. Quoted: 'my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; the assumption about culture in Marx's 'capital' and 'labor history in general' (p. xi); 'an extended polemic against the reductionism'; 'Culture ... is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii); capitalism's 'need or capacity to homogenize' (p. xiii); 'citizen' and 'comrade' (p. xiv); the worker of Marx's assumption and the bourgeois notion of equality (p. 3); 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9); no 'working class' that runs 'in its empty sameness throughout the course of history' (p. 6). Eric Hobsbawm, Sumit Sarkar and others are thanked as readers of the manuscript (p. xvii). Chapters 2–7 remain unread.

sarkar_decline.note: Scan OCR'd locally and pp. 84–85, 87 and 97 checked against the page images for the 1.132 person entry. Quoted: Chakrabarty's summary of a shift from 'to write “better” Marxist histories' to the problem of 'universalism/Eurocentrism' (pp. 84–85; Sarkar's n. 5 cites Chakrabarty's 'Marx after Marxism', unread); 'the trajectory that has been outlined with considerable precision and frankness by Chakrabarty has been debilitating in both academic and political terms' (p. 85); 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history' (p. 87); on kula and grihalaksmi, 'Beauty, pleasure, the good life ... for whom, it is surely legitimate to ask' (p. 97).
